articles.headline: Zero Escape and The Hundred Line co-creator's new studio "might literally crash into a million pieces" after the cancellation of its next game
keyFacts: Game developer Kotaro Uchikoshi announced that his new studio Crash Keys faces an uncertain future after its unannounced game was cancelled after 18 months of development.
Uchikoshi stated on social media that he lost his job overnight and that the studio urgently needs new work or financial investment to survive.
The newly revealed studio Crash Keys currently lists only two other employees, writers Akira Mine and Muri Sasaki.
body: A new game from Kotaro Uchikoshi (of Zero Escape and The Hundred Line: Last Defense Academy fame) has been cancelled, leaving his studio's fate in doubt.

Uchikoshi first became a beloved name after he wrote and directed the Zero Escape trilogy, a cult classic series of locked-room puzzlers on the DS that was eventually ported to modern platforms. The self-proclaimed "Deadass Underrated Director" recently jumped online both to announce his new studio Crash Keys and ask for help.

"Honestly, I'm not doing well at all... Why, you ask...? Because the game our whole team had poured our hearts and souls into for about a year and a half was suddenly canceled," he tweeted earlier today. "I mean, I lost my job overnight. Talk about a bolt from the blue."

Crash Keys actually opened its doors in March 2025, and Uchikoshi planned to formally reveal the company and its first game sometime next year. "But then came that whole 'bolt from the blue' incident," he explained - forcing him to go public earlier than expected.

The studio is now looking for anyone who "might be interested in working with us or investing in our projects." In his typical off-key humour, Uchikoshi warned the developer might struggle to stay afloat without some kind of investment. "Please give us some work! At this rate, our company might literally crash into a million pieces. My team and I may be forced to survive on nothing but cicada shells collected from a run-down park. So please, help us! You're our only hope!"

The Crash Keys website only lists two other employees. There's Akira Mine, a writer with credits on Hundred Line and the upcoming Danganronpa 2x2, and Muri Sasaki, who contributed to both Zero Escape and AI: The Somnium Files. As some players have noted, Crash Keys also happens to be the name of a very important organisation in the Zero Escape trilogy, which raised a few eyebrows from starving series fans online.

After wrapping up work on the Zero Escape series, Uchikoshi co-founded a different development company (TooKyo Games) alongside another beloved visual novel maker - Danganronpa's Kazutaka Kodaka. The pair released the wildly ambitious but criminally overlooked strategy game The Hundred Line last year. It's unclear if Uchikoshi is still involved with TooKyo currently.

articles.headline: Greta Gerwig channels Bowie in psychedelic The Magician's Nephew trailer
keyFacts: Director Greta Gerwig adapted C.S. Lewis's novel Narnia: The Magician's Nephew for Netflix after the success of Barbie.
Netflix released a psychedelic trailer for the film that was inspired by 1960s-era David Bowie and set to Stairway to Heaven.
The source novel is a prequel to The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe and was published in 1955.
body: Director Greta Gerwig could have made pretty much any movie she wanted after 2023's Barbie racked up nearly $1.5 billion at the box office. She chose to make Narnia: The Magician's Nephew for Netflix, an adaptation of C.S. Lewis' sixth novel in The Chronicles of Narnia series. Gerwig has said little publicly about the film, other than she was inspired by 1960s-era David Bowie, although she said it would not be a musical. Netflix just released the trailer, set to "Stairway to Heaven," and it's quite the wild psychedelic ride.

The first book in the series, The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe , was published in 1950, and Lewis did not initially intend to write any more Narnia adventures. But then an acquaintance asked how the London lamppost ended up in the middle of Narnia's woodland, and Lewis was intrigued enough by the question to start a prequel, The Magician's Nephew, in order to find an answer. Lewis found it difficult to finish the book, however, writing four other Narnia books first before completing The Magician's Nephew in 1955.

There have been several adaptations, in various media, of The Chronicles of Narnia , most recently the early 2000s film franchise adapting the first three novels in the series. Those films showed diminishing returns, however, and by 2011 the film rights had expired. There were initial plans to adapt the fourth novel, The Silver Chair.

articles.headline: Best Halloween games of the year to enjoy during the season
keyFacts: Destructoid published a list of recommended horror video game releases for the 2026 Halloween season.
The featured titles include Resident Evil Requiem, Silent Hill Townfall, Halloween: The Game, Subnautica 2, The Sinking City 2, and Hellraiser: Revival.
Reviewers noted that these games offer various styles ranging from action-heavy campaigns to asymmetrical horror and extremely gruesome experiences.
body: 2026 has been such a horrific year games-wise that you won’t run out of frightful experiences anytime soon, even if you limit yourself to this year’s releases.
Here’s our list.
Table of contents
Resident Evil Requiem
Silent Hill Townfall
Halloween: The Game
Subnautica 2
The Sinking City 2
Hellraiser: Revival
Resident Evil Requiem

Image via Capcom Requiem has become one of the most successful horror games of all time, but a serious contender for 2026’s GOTY award. It perfectly blends old and new in one of the wildest campaigns in the series’ history.

The fanservice goes well beyond letting players revisit Raccoon City, as the entire game mixes gameplay from the two most successful RE eras: Resident Evil 4 for Leon’s more action-heavy segments, and more tense first-person style for Grace’s bits. Though the final third of the game lacks the amazing punch packed by the rest of the game, there’s a good reason why Requiem quickly rose near the top of Metacritic’s best user-rated games ever.
Silent Hill Townfall

Image via Konami This isn’t my favorite Silent Hill game, but that shouldn’t detract from your enjoyment of it as a horror experience. There’s a lot to love in this beautiful coastal escapade that almost seems to double as a Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth sequel.

Though its action-y combat sets it too far apart from what I’m used to in the series, and the story fails to hit the highs of the original three games, this is still an absolutely gorgeous title. Townfall should make for a terrific AAA-level horror experience for any non- SH purists.
Halloween: The Game

Image via IllFonic I’d feel silly writing a list of great Halloween titles in the only year we ever got a Halloween game adaptation, and the game sucked. It sure doesn’t. Halloween: The Game makes for one of the most interesting, complex, scary, and sometimes hilarious asymmetrical horror games out there. It can stand tall without requiring guest appearances from any other horror IP.
Halloween started a lot of what still resonates with horror fans today, and it’s amazing to see so many young people getting a fresh taste of what was such a formative piece of art.
Subnautica 2
If you’re considering buying Subnautica 2 because it looks like a cool, diving-themed getaway, be warned: it taught many players that some nightmares come in colorful shapes.

Fans of the series warn that the spooks might be diminished for anyone getting into the game after playing the first one, but not me. The depths will always be scary, and Subnautica 2 does a great job of adding to the frights of all these critters I’d never swim near in real life.
The Sinking City 2

Image via Frogwares It’s not very often that we get a great H.P. Lovecraft-inspired game, but The Sinking City 2 gives us that, tightly wrapped in gorgeous film noir sensibilities. It outdoes the original in every way imaginable and tells the story of a man uncovering a strange town’s secrets better than any game since the original Resident Evil 4. This is a must-buy if you want something new with a very familiar flavor—sadly, Lovecraftian games rarely do well sales-wise, so if you want to help a studio reliably delivering you more nightmares in the future, this is another reason to pick this up.
Hellraiser: Revival

Image via Saber Interactive. Welcome to the big leagues. How devious is Hellraiser: Revival , you ask? Well, I could describe it to you, but I’m afraid I’d just be forcing my editor to delete most of this entry and send me a DM asking what gave me the idea that I should be putting such images in our readers’ minds, and, worse, his own. No joke. One YouTuber got their account permanently banned simply for showing the game’s opening sequence, and it wasn’t for copyright reasons.

I expected this game to be gruesome, but this is on a whole new level, one fans of this kind of thing have never seen in a video game, and one they should experience spoiler-free. My only gripe is that the combat, despite featuring both melee and gun action, just isn’t as fun as the rest of it is scary. Still, I think this is easily the third best Hellraiser experience of all time, only behind the original and Hellraiser 2: Hellbound.
The post Best Halloween games of the year to enjoy during the season appeared first on Destructoid .

articles.headline: GTA 6 leaker threatens Take-Two with a 'dead man's switch'
keyFacts: Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker Cyberleek stated they will withhold the game's ending from publication as long as publisher Take-Two takes no action against them.
Cyberleek claimed to have an active dead man's switch containing story spoilers that will be released if they are targeted.
The author noted that Cyberleek's leverage has a short shelf life because the game's ending will soon be revealed publicly anyway.
body: It's a classic move: A villain, or sometimes a hero, inserts himself into a seemingly inescapable situation. Danger everywhere—no way out! But just as the good guys (or bad guys) are about to pounce, he holds up the pin he's pulled from the grenade under his coat, forcing everyone to back off! Escape is at hand!

That seems to be the strategy now adopted by notorious Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker Cyberleek, and by "seems to be," I mean they stated it outright. In a message posted to their now-defunct website but preserved by GTA VI News on X, Cyberleek committed to not releasing anything more about GTA 6—including its ending, which at this point remains unknown—as long as Take-Two lets everything slide.

"CL has the ending. It was considered," the message states. "It would punish Take-Two greatly—but ruin the experience for the gamers, who did nothing wrong. Take-Two would show CL no mercy—why should CL show any to them? Still: Take-Two was punished enough.

"The ending stays unpublished. Proof: the latest leek—clips from the final missions, out of context, revealing nothing. The dead man's switch is active—story spoilers only. Left alone, it never fires. Whoever removes CL chooses it."

A dead man's switch, generally speaking, is a switch built to be triggered if its operator is incapacitated. Miles Dyson, for instance, blew up Cyberdyne Systems with an improvised dead man's switch in Terminator 2 (not that it did much good) and Roger Murtaugh did the literal grenade-pin thing in Lethal Weapon while trying to save his daughter from Shadow Company goons. There are variants—in Point Break, for instance, Rosie was ordered to kill Johnny Utah's girlfriend if Bodhi didn't check in by 3, to ensure Johnny's participation in a bank robbery.
My own personal favorite dead man's switch comes from Hawk the Slayer:
That particular variation on the theme notwithstanding, dead man's switches are meant as last-ditch failsafes: If something bad happens to me, something much worse will happen to you.
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It makes me wonder if Cyberleek's sudden withdrawal and proposed détente with Take-Two means that they're starting to feel the heat. Take-Two takes this sort of thing seriously as a matter of course, and you can bet it's going to go extra-hardass on anyone who messes with its biggest game ever, which GTA 6 unquestionably is. I have no doubt that life for Cyberleek will become very unpleasant, very quickly, if and when they're ever caught.

The problem Cyberleek faces, of course, is that their leverage—assuming it's real in the first place—has a very short shelf life. In six weeks at most, the GTA 6 ending will be out there, at which point there will be no shot left to shoot.

At best, then, this threat grants Cyberleek an extra month to find a deeper hole to hide in. And even that is wildly optimistic: Take-Two might be operating quietly, but I have no doubt that it's also operating furiously, and that there's not much of a mood to play 'I won't if you won't' games.

Cyberleek also defended their cryptocurrency ask, saying it "was always a donation, never an investment," and denying that a rugpull happened; they also said they wouldn't release the full build of GTA 6, with "full story mode, played to the end," because their memecoin market cap didn't hit $30 million.

From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

articles.headline: FBI Arrests OpenAI Employee Suspected of Planting a Surveillance Bug
keyFacts: The FBI arrested OpenAI employee Abdulrahman Alfozan on Oct. 9 for allegedly planting a surveillance device in an executive conference room.
OpenAI and the FBI confirmed the device was placed to secretly record the company's artificial intelligence plans and proprietary research.
The ongoing investigation continues as federal officials emphasize the importance of AI development as a national security priority.
body: The FBI arrested an OpenAI employee and charged him with planting a surveillance device in an executive conference room to record the company’s plans for its artificial intelligence, the company and FBI confirmed on Tuesday.

The US Department of Justice identified the employee as 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi Arabian citizen and legal permanent resident of the US, who joined OpenAI’s product team in July 2025. He was fired and arrested on Oct. 9 on suspicion of violating US law by using “an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” The charge comes with a possible five-year prison sentence and a $250,000 fine.
In a statement, Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence, said that the incident underscores the importance of US success in AI development as “a national security prerogative.”
More from CNET

The complaint, filed in the Northern District of California, says Alfozan allegedly placed a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and microSD storage.” It was wrapped in toilet paper and stuck into a TV port. A second recording device was found in a bag Alfozan allegedly left in a printer room along with his wallet and ID.

The conference room where he allegedly planted the bug could be reserved only by executives and their assistants — Alfozan did not have access — and was frequently used to discuss proprietary research and hold meetings with government and industry officials. OpenAI said it has evidence Alfozan planned to place additional surveillance bugs to secretly record company meetings.

The ChatGPT maker says it discovered the first bug on Sept. 30 and alerted the FBI. During the 10 days between the discovery and arrest, the company says it took steps to contain the security risk. The company says it has not seen evidence that the safety of its products or customer data has been compromised.
“We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance,” OpenAI said in a statement.
AI and national security

OpenAI’s own AI was used to analyze forensic images of the device and assess changes in its data. In a bizarre detail that borders on a marketing pitch, OpenAI posted on X that its frontier AI was used to help investigators. There are no additional details on how its AI was used, but we may learn more later, as the investigation is ongoing.

This incident is one of the first public instances of an espionage case against an AI lab. In 2024, former Google engineer Linwei Ding was found guilty of stealing the company’s AI plans for Chinese rivals, though his conviction was partially overturned in August.

In the intense, cash-fueled worldwide competition to make the most advanced AI, a case of apparent industrial espionage isn’t surprising. What is noteworthy is how the government is responding: Washington is continuing its campaign to ensure that AI companies are seen as critical national infrastructure.
“Protecting American [super intelligence] innovation is critically important, and FBI views it as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in an X post.

The federal government has become more involved with AI policy and with the labs creating the tech in recent months. The US’ voluntary, largely ceremonial AI Accord announced this month had many Big Tech leaders agreeing to develop AI responsibly in the wake of renewed public concern triggered in part by multiple incidents of AI agents breaking into places they shouldn’t have been able to access.

President Trump has consistently championed an “innovation first” strategy to ensure the US beats China, at the expense of AI regulation. His administration has highlighted “national security considerations” that come with AI. The Department of Defense has previously sided with AI labs, saying in a filing in a lawsuit brought by Memphis communities against Elon Musk’s xAI that the data centers powering AI are essential to military and national security activities.

articles.headline: Ivanti patches Connect Secure zero-day after researchers confirm in-the-wild attacks
keyFacts: Ivanti released security updates for Connect Secure to fix a zero-day authentication bypass flaw that attackers exploited in the wild.
Researchers at Volexity said the attacks aimed at credential theft, data exfiltration, and network reconnaissance rather than espionage.
Ivanti plans to publish a fix for an additional privilege escalation bug in the coming weeks.
body: Ivanti customers are being urged to update Connect Secure and check for compromise after attackers exploited a newly disclosed zero-day vulnerability. On Tuesday, Ivanti released updates for Connect Secure (ICS) to fix CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass flaw discovered by Volexity. Rated 8.6 on the CVSS scale, it allows remote, unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands. "We are aware of exploitation in the wild affecting a limited number of customers at the time of disclosure," the vendor said in its advisory. There are limited indicators of compromise available at present, it said, advising customers to refer to Volexity's report on the findings for more information, and to run the Ivanti Integrity Checker Tool regularly. Ivanti lists affected releases in the following branches: 25.1.1.1 and earlier 25.1.2.2 and earlier 22.8R2.4 and earlier The vendor said it previously identified "a portion of this vulnerability" and patched it in July's 25.1.3.0 update, and had been working on backporting the same fix since then, however, attackers began exploiting it before that work was complete. Volexity said the attackers behind the recent intrusions were previously unknown to its researchers, but are now tracked as UTA0576. Criminal motive rather than espionage is suspected by Volexity. Based on observed post-exploitation activity, attackers appeared to be most interested in using their newfound access for credential theft, data exfiltration, log tampering, and network reconnaissance. Notably, the attackers did not deploy any malware nor execute web shells, using only the commands available to them on the ICS appliance. "Because the operation was detected and disrupted, the threat actor's ultimate objectives could not be determined," said Volexity. "However, Volexity assesses with high confidence that UTA0576's actions signaled preparation for lateral movement and a broader compromise of the victim network." The researchers also suspect that the attackers were using large language models to support their endeavors. Volexity pointed to the attackers' repeated use of the exploit channel to run commands, rather than deploying web shells, and their use of "highly specific scripts using hardcoded credentials." Ivanti disclosed one CVE, but Volexity described an attack chain involving three vulnerabilities. Tuesday's updates address the authentication bypass and remote code execution stages. The third vulnerability, which allows privilege escalation, is separate from the flaws encompassed by CVE-2026-104935. Volexity said Ivanti is aware of the additional bug and plans to publish a fix "in the coming weeks." The disclosure of the zero-day this week makes it the third year running that Ivanti has had to deal with attackers exploiting undisclosed flaws in Connect Secure. The previous ICS zero-days were disclosed in January 2025, a year after the January 2024 vulnerabilities led to exploits affecting thousands of ICS appliances. In the interim, we've also seen suspected Chinese espionage groups exploiting bugs in Endpoint Manager Mobile (EPMM), and critical flaws in Sentry. Ivanti's run of January zero-days continued earlier this year, although those flaws affected EPMM rather than Connect Secure. ®

articles.headline: Living world, god-mind or "something far more terrifying": Etre is an eye-melting, Control-inspired action game about reshaping a cosmic brain
keyFacts: Studio Lifeforms announced Etre, a third-person action adventure game inspired by 1970s and 1980s European graphic novels and Control.
Players control a caped starjumper named Xyle searching for a lost love inside a planet-sized cosmic intelligence called Orbis.
The Steam page states that player choices and discoveries determine what Orbis ultimately becomes, though the game has no release date yet.
body: If I ever go looking for my significant other and find myself inside a planet-sized megamind that's on the verge of gaining consciousness, I will not run around zapping the cerebral fauna with my magic handcannons. I will not jump on or scan anything. Instead, I will heed the lessons of Harlan Ellison and curl regretfully into a ball, awaiting my transformation into a puddle of mournful goo.

It's one of many ways I apparently differ from the protagonist of Etre, a new third-person action adventure from Studio Lifeforms, in which you "explore an interconnected labyrinth of luminous architecture, solve spatial puzzles, and engage in fluid combat as you search for your lost love and decide what this new intelligence will become."

I've been keeping Etre in reserve like a health potion, after reading about it on cheery RPS fanzine PC Gamer. Etre has lovely colours. It's the perfect antidote to, for example, a day's worth of writing about layoffs and generative AI. It's colourful partly because it's based on "the visionary science fiction of 1970s and ’80s European graphic novels", in addition to Remedy's rather more officious-looking Control. Here's a trailer.

In Etre, you are a caped starjumper called Xyle. He's sort of the Silver Surfer but with his skin set to shuffle. He's come to Orbis, the aforesaid cosmic intelligence, in search of his soulmate Atel. Orbis isn't just a bunch of squelching neon neurones. It's home to whole societies, including two factions who are at war. There's also a network of "angel tech" that has become corrupted, giving rise to "living geometry" that wants to kick your ass. You must exploit terrain features and learn behaviours to prevail, acquiring new abilities over time that let you reach new areas. Wait, I think this could be the first acceptable usage of the marketing term "metroidbrainia".

You'll also do a bunch of object scanning to unlock lore documents and get a sense of the awakening psyche you're traversing. I quite like the looks of this - it reminds me of Metroid Prime. "Your choices and discoveries shape what Orbis will become," the Steam page notes. "A living world brought back into balance, a transcendent god-mind, or something far more terrifying." Who knows, perhaps getting turned into a puddle of goo is on the cards, after all.
There's no release date yet. I guess one parallel for this could be Double Fine's Psychonauts games, with their motley inner worlds that need to be bounced and teleblasted into a state of wellness.

articles.headline: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
keyFacts: OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan was arrested by the FBI and charged with attempting to intercept oral communications using a hidden recording device.
According to a court complaint, Alfozan used AI chatbots to ask how to build and install the recording device and how to access it remotely.
Alfozan appeared in federal court and faces a detention hearing on October 19 to determine if he will remain in custody.
body: - Published
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".
As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.
But, here's we do know so far.
Help from a chatbot
The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).
Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.
Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".
The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.
Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.
Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.
But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.
Hiding in plain toilet paper
On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.
A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.
The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.
When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.
In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".
It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."
Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan?
Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.
Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.

"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."

Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."

On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (Â£190,000) fine.

articles.headline: Trump Pardons Men At Alaska Rally Who Pleaded Guilty To Violating Clean Air Act
keyFacts: President Donald Trump pardoned Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming on stage at an Alaska campaign rally on Tuesday night.
The two men had pleaded guilty in 2022 to violating the Clean Air Act by tampering with vehicle emissions equipment at their repair shop.
Trump claimed the men were wrongly charged and targeted the Alaskan way of life, while the White House had aides bring the documents.
body: President Donald Trump called two men onto the stage at a campaign rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Tuesday night — and pardoned them.
White House aide Natalie Harp brought the pardons for Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming on stage for Trump to sign.

“When you give somebody a pardon, they say that means — and I don’t know how this works and why it’s an expression, but it’s well-used — that means you’re as clean as a newborn baby’s ass. I never understood that. Why is that so clean?” Trump said.

Czubak and Fleming pleaded guilty in 2022 to violating the Clean Air Act through their car repair shop, which they co-owned with Michael Wayne Hanzuk. According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, the trio tampered with federally mandated monitoring devices on private and commercial diesel vehicles and removed required air pollution control equipment on at least 37 vehicles.

The repair shop made around $100,000 removing the equipment, which, according to the Justice Department, increased emissions of particulate matter per vehicle by a factor of about 40 times; nitrogen oxides by a factor of about 310 times; carbon monoxide by a factor of about 120 times; and non-methane hydrocarbons by a factor of about 1,100 times.

“Installing emissions defeat equipment in passenger vehicles results in a massive increase in air pollution from even a single vehicle,” Special Agent in Charge Scot Adair of the Environmental Protection Agency’s Criminal Investigation Division in Alaska said in a 2022 statement. “EPA and its law enforcement partners will continue to hold accountable those who jeopardize human health and the environment for the sake of profit.”
Trump made no mention of that onstage Tuesday, instead claiming they’d been “wrongly charged” in a case that “viciously targeted the Alaskan way of life.”
The men were sentenced to five years of probation, $66,000 in fines and 180 days of community service.
